source_text: Υἱὸς δὲ θεοῦ, ὁ Ιησοῦς λεγόμενος, εἰ καὶ κοινῶς μόνον ἄνθρωπος, διὰ σοφίαν ἄξιος υἱὸς θεοῦ λέγεσθαι· πατέρα γὰρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε πάντες συγγραφεῖς τὸν θεὸν καλοῦσιν. Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἰδίως, παρὰ τὴν κοινὴν γένεσιν, γεγεννῆσθαι αὐτὸν ἐκ θεοῦ λέγομεν λόγον θεοῦ, ὡς προέφημεν, κοινὸν τοῦτο ἔστω ὑμῖν τοῖς τὸν Ἑρμῆν λόγον τὸν παρὰ θεοῦ ἀγγελτικὸν λέγουσιν. Εἰ δὲ αἰτιάσαιτό τις ἐσταυρῶσθαι αὐτόν, καὶ τοῦτο κοινὸν τοῖς προκατηριθμημένοις παθοῦσιν υἱοῖς καθ᾿ ὑμᾶς τοῖ Διὸς ὑπάρχει. Ἐκείνων τε γὰρ οὐχ ὅμοια τὰ πάθη τοῦ θανάτου ἀλλὰ διάφορα ἱστορεῖται· ὥστε μηδὲ τὸ ἴδιον τοῦ πάθους ἥττονα δοκεῖν εἶναι τοῦτον, ἀλλ᾿, ὡς ὑπεσχόμεθα, προϊόντος τοῦ λόγου καὶ κρείττονα ἀποδείξομεν, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἀποδέδεικται· ὁ γὰρ κρείττων ἐκ τῶν πράξεων φαίνεται. Εἰ δὲ καὶ διὰ παρθένου γεγεννῆσθαι φέρομεν, κοινὸν καὶ τοῦτο πρὸς τὸν Περσέα ἔστω ὑμῖν. Ὧι δὲ λέγομεν χωλοὺς καὶ παραλυτικοὺς καὶ ἐκ γενετῆς πονηροὺς ὑγιεῖς πεποιηκέναι αὐτὸν καὶ νεκροὺς ἀνεγεῖραι, ὅμοια τοῖς ὑπὸ Ἀσκληπιοῦ γεγενῆσθαι λεγομένοις καὶ ταῦτα φάσκειν δόξομεν.
pass_a_gloss: But the Jesus who is called Son of God, even if he is only a man in a common way, is worthy to be called Son of God because of his wisdom; for all writers call God the father of men and gods. But if we also say that he was begotten from God in a special way, apart from common birth, and that he is the Word of God, as we said before, let this be common to you who say that Hermes is the word of God, the messenger from God. And if someone were to blame him for being crucified, this also is common to the sons who suffered beforehand according to you, who belong to Zeus. For the sufferings of death of those are not told as being similar, but as being different; so that the special nature of his suffering should not seem to be less, but, as we promised, as the discourse proceeds, we will demonstrate it to be even greater, or rather, it has already been demonstrated; for the greater one is shown by his actions. And if we also say that he was born from a virgin, let this also be common to Perseus. And when we say that he made the lame and the paralyzed and those born with defects healthy, and raised the dead, we will seem to be saying things similar to those said to have been done by Asclepius.

pass_b_english: Even if the Jesus who is called Son of God were merely a man in the ordinary sense, he would still be worthy of that title because of his wisdom; after all, every writer calls God the father of both men and gods. But if we also say that he was begotten from God in a unique way, distinct from ordinary birth, and that he is the Word of God — as we said before — let this be common ground with you who claim that Hermes is the Word of God, the messenger from God. And if anyone objects to his crucifixion, that too is common ground with the sons who suffered beforehand, according to your tradition, who belong to Zeus. For the sufferings of death among those figures are not told as similar but as different; therefore, the unique character of his suffering should not be thought lesser. Instead, as we promised, as the argument proceeds we will demonstrate it to be even greater — indeed, it has already been demonstrated, for the greater one is revealed by his actions. And if we also say that he was born of a virgin, let that also be common ground with Perseus. And when we say that he made the lame, the paralyzed, and those born with defects healthy, and raised the dead, we will appear to be saying things similar to what is said to have been done by Asclepius.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the distinctions between 'common' (κοινῶς/κοινὸν) and 'special/unique' (ἰδίως) modes of being/birth, and the comparison to mythological figures (Hermes, Zeus's sons, Perseus, Asclepius). Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.

The Greek text is correctly identified as Justin's First Apology 22. The translation preserves the original meaning, including the use of 'Son of God,' 'wisdom,' 'Word of God,' and references to Hermes, Perseus, and Asclepius. All key terms are accurately translated, and the scriptural and cultural allusions are preserved. The text is complete and faithful to the source.
